title: An object to remember
hookLine: Stoics, monks and painters kept a skull or a small object as a reminder
carry: a knot tied in a handkerchief

lines: A CANDLE, AN HOURGLASS, A SKULL.
AN OBJECT THAT REMEMBERS FOR YOU.
cards: A desk in an old Dutch painting. A book left open. A candle burned down to a stub.
An hourglass with most of the sand at the bottom. A pocket watch. And, sitting calmly among them, a human skull.
Painters made whole still lifes like this, and art historians call them vanitas paintings, from the Latin for vanity, the word that echoes through Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
They weren't horror pictures. They were reminders, made to hang where someone would see them every day. Today: the small object that does the remembering for you.

teach.b: First, the skull on the desk. In those paintings the objects talk to each other. The candle is burning, the sand is falling, the flowers are about to drop their petals.
The skull just says it plainly. The Latin phrase people attach to these pictures is memento mori: remember that you will die. Second, death before your eyes.
In the Handbook of the Stoic teacher Epictetus, the advice, in paraphrase, is to keep death and every other thing that seems terrible before your eyes daily, and death most of all.
Then, he says, you'll never think a mean thought or crave anything beyond measure. For him, the reminder wasn't gloom. It kept desire the right size.
Third, a skull in a play. In Shakespeare, the gravedigger hands Hamlet a skull, and Hamlet learns whose it was: the jester he loved as a boy.

"Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio." The scene turns a bone into a person, and a person into a question. Tradition says some monks kept a skull in their cells for the same reason; others kept a cross, or a few beads.
Fourth, any small object will do.
None of these is magic. A skull, a coin, a smooth stone, a dried leaf: each works like a knot tied in a handkerchief.
Set it where your eye lands, and it quietly asks the question for you on the days you'd forget to ask it yourself.

how: Some people keep a small object on a desk or in a pocket as a memento mori, a reminder of death that keeps the day in proportion; in some traditions it has been a skull, a cross or prayer beads.

games.q: you're Hamlet. the gravedigger tosses up a skull and tells you whose it was. what do you say?
o: Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio.
you ask for a different grave.
games.why: Hamlet recognizes the jester he loved as a boy, and the bone becomes a person.

practice: Choose one small object near you, a stone, a key, a coin, a leaf, a photograph; it doesn't need to be grim. Hold it, or rest your eyes on it, and let it mean one simple thing: this day is not forever, so let it count.
Breathe with it a while, and decide where it might live, somewhere your eye will land without trying.

wordCard.voice: Memento mori, Latin for remember that you will die, the phrase behind the painter's skull and Epictetus's daily reminder. Today's word.
